wine.name: Romanée-Conti
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Nuits, held whole by the domaine as a monopole
wine.sites: The single small vineyard of Romanée-Conti in the middle of the Vosne-Romanée slope, with La Romanée above it, Richebourg to the north, La Grande Rue to the south and Romanée-Saint-Vivant below.
wine.making: Fermented in wooden vats over a long cuvaison of up to a month, in most vintages wholly as whole bunches with the stems kept. The wine is aged in new oak barrels for sixteen to twenty months and bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Rose petal, red cherry and wild strawberry over Chinese five spice, orange peel and forest floor; light in body yet deep, with silken, fine tannin and a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Supple enough to taste young but at its fullest after fifteen to twenty years, and a strong vintage lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant only to take an old bottle off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The grand cru, its own appellation; the vineyard's name stands alone, with no village.
The label names the owner, the Société Civile du Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, which has held the domaine since 1942.
The count of bottles the vintage gave, printed with this bottle's own number.

records.table: Named for the Prince de Conti, who bought it in 1760, Romanée-Conti is the monopole of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, a single small grand cru in the middle of the Vosne-Romanée slope. Light in body yet long and perfumed, it wants a wide glass and time.
records.story: The priory of Saint-Vivant held this vineyard in the Middle Ages, and by the middle of the seventeenth century it was known as La Romanée, for a reason nobody has found. In 1760 it was bought by Louis François de Bourbon, Prince de Conti (1717 to 1776), and the vineyard came to carry his name; the tale that he outbid the King's favourite for it is doubted. The Revolution seized it from his son, and in 1794 it was sold at auction. In 1869 it was bought by a wine merchant whose heirs, the de Villaine family among them, built the domaine around it, and in 1933 the domaine bought the rest of La Tâche at the auction of the Liger-Belair estate, which made it a second monopole. In 1942 the domaine became a société civile, and the Leroy family bought half of it. Romanée-Conti kept its ungrafted vines through phylloxera until the harvest of 1945; they were then pulled up, the vineyard was replanted in 1947, and the next Romanée-Conti was the 1952 vintage. For a sommelier it is the name every guest knows and few have tasted: a grand cru held whole by one domaine, light and endless rather than powerful.

wine.name: Chambertin
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Nuits
wine.sites: Parcels of Chambertin, the grand cru of the Gevrey slope between Chambertin-Clos de Bèze to the north and Latricières-Chambertin to the south, with Griotte-Chambertin and Charmes-Chambertin below it to the east.
wine.making: The grapes are sorted as they reach the cellar and fermented at the domaine. The wine is then aged for well over a year in oak barrels that are all new, as only the Chambertin and the Clos de Bèze are each year, the house's other wines taking less new wood, and is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Black cherry, liquorice and violet over iron, game and a savoury, earthy depth; firm, fine tannin and a long, deep finish, more power than charm when young.
wine.ageing: Tight and tannic for ten years or more, it opens slowly and lasts for decades in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one only off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The grand cru, its own appellation; the vineyard's name stands alone, with no village.
The rank above Premier Cru, printed with the vineyard's name.
The house, named for the founder who began to bottle his own wine in the 1930s.

records.table: From the Gevrey grand cru that lies between Clos de Bèze and Latricières, Domaine Armand Rousseau's Chambertin is raised wholly in new oak, as its Clos de Bèze is. Dense, firm and savoury, and slower to open than that neighbour, it repays a decanter and a long wait.
records.story: Gevrey's great vineyard began with its neighbour: in 640, as the Bourgogne wine body records it, a duke gave a clos here to the monks of the abbey of Bèze, and Chambertin, the story goes, is the field of a man named Bertin who planted beside them, the champ de Bertin, a name in the records by the thirteenth century. Napoleon, as the legend tells it, drank its wine with water at his meals. In 1847 the village of Gevrey added the vineyard's name to its own. Armand Rousseau (1884 to 1959) came into a house and his first vines in Gevrey with his marriage in 1909, and he bought parcels of the grands crus, Mazis-Chambertin in 1937 among them. In the 1930s, urged on by the editor of the Revue du Vin de France, he began to bottle and sell his own wine, among the first growers of the Côte d'Or to do so, when most sold their wine in cask to the merchants. His son Charles, who died in 2016, took charge in 1959 and widened the holdings. Chambertin, firmer and slower than the house's Clos de Bèze, shows the domaine's method plainest: every barrel new, and patience.

wine.name: Musigny Grand Cru Vieilles Vignes
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Nuits
wine.sites: The domaine's larger part of Musigny, Les Petits Musigny entire among it, at the southern end of Chambolle above the Clos de Vougeot; only vines of twenty five years and more go into this wine.
wine.making: Fermented in vats and aged in oak barrels, a third or a little more of them new, for well over a year before bottling at the domaine. Musigny vines younger than twenty five years go into the domaine's Chambolle-Musigny Premier Cru instead.
wine.glass: Red and black cherry, violet and rose over iron, liquorice and forest floor; silken and perfumed yet firmly built, with fine tannin and a long, slow finish.
wine.ageing: Reserved and tightly wound young, it shows its perfume only after a decade in bottle and lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Only the older vines of de Vogüé's large share of Musigny, the grand cru at the southern end of Chambolle, go into its Musigny Vieilles Vignes. Reserved and tightly wound young, silken and perfumed with age, it rewards a decade's patience.
records.story: The family's vines in Chambolle go back to 1450, and the estate passed down by descent and by marriage until, in 1766, a marriage brought it into the de Vogüé family. Comte Georges de Vogüé inherited it from his father in 1925, gave it the name it bears and ran it until his death in 1987. The domaine holds the larger part of the grand cru Musigny, Les Petits Musigny entire. Musigny is also the one grand cru of the Côte de Nuits with a white wine, and de Vogüé is its maker. After a replanting in the late 1980s and the 1990s, the domaine sold that white as Bourgogne Blanc from the 1994 vintage, and the Musigny name returned to its label with the 2015 vintage. Only vines of twenty five years and more go into Musigny Vieilles Vignes; the younger make the domaine's Chambolle premier cru, so the grand cru carries the depth of old roots. Slow and structured, the face of Chambolle's perfume that opens only after ten years, it shows beside the house's Bonnes-Mares how one village can give two such different grands crus.

wine.name: Bonnes-Mares
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Nuits
wine.sites: Two parcels of Bonnes-Mares, one in the terres blanches of pale, chalky marl high on the slope and one in the terres rouges of reddish clay lower down, in the grand cru that runs from Chambolle-Musigny into Morey-Saint-Denis.
wine.making: Partly destemmed, with a share of whole bunches that changes with the vintage, often a third or more. The two parcels are fermented and aged apart, in oak barrels a third to a half of them new, for fourteen to eighteen months, then blended and bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Black cherry, red currant and rose stem over crushed stone and a savoury earthiness; dense and firm for Chambolle, with fine, grippy tannin and a long, cool finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed young, it needs ten to fifteen years in bottle and lasts well beyond.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The grand cru, its own appellation, shared between Chambolle-Musigny and Morey-Saint-Denis.
The rank above Premier Cru, printed with the vineyard's name.

records.table: Drawn from two parcels of Bonnes-Mares, one on pale marl high on the slope and one on red clay below, Domaine Georges Roumier's wine is firmer and darker than most Chambolle. It is slow to open, so keep it ten years and pour it with game.
records.story: Bonnes-Mares runs along the slope from Chambolle-Musigny into Morey-Saint-Denis, and its name is read either as the good mothers, the Cistercian nuns of Tart who held vines here from the twelfth century, or as marer, an old word for tilling the ground. The domaine dates from 1924, when its founder married into a Chambolle family and his wife's dowry of vines came with her. In 1945 he began to bottle part of his wine at the domaine, when most growers sold theirs in cask to the merchants. The founder's son took over in the 1960s, and the founder's grandson joined him in the early 1980s. Under the family the style has stayed fine and cool: a share of whole bunches, some new oak and no more. The domaine also holds Clos de la Bussière, a premier cru in Morey-Saint-Denis, whole. Bonnes-Mares shows the house plainly, because its two parcels lie on two soils, pale marl high on the slope and red clay below, and the domaine raises them apart before it blends them. Explain those two soils to a guest and you have explained why one vineyard can give two textures in a single wine.

report: Rechecked with search on 12 November 2026: the founding of 1924 by marriage, the dowry of Chambolle vines and the first bottling at the domaine in 1945 rest on Decanter, Christie's and Vinous, read through search; one account says full domaine bottling came only in 1984.
The son took over in 1961 by Decanter's account and his father died in 1965 by another, so the story says the 1960s; the grandson joined in 1981, 1982 or 1984 by the accounts, so the early 1980s.

The two parcels, the terres blanches high on the slope and the terres rouges below, fermented and aged apart and blended before bottling, and the share of whole bunches and new oak, rest on Leon and Son's listings, the World of Fine Wine and Decanter, which disagree on the figures, so the record gives ranges.
The two readings of the name Bonnes-Mares rest on Wikipedia, the Domaine de la Vougeraie sheet and Joseph Drouhin.

Clos de la Bussière was bought in 1953 by Decanter's account (from the Bettenfeld family) and one writer's wiki; with no second source the year is left out. Vinous puts part of Bonnes-Mares in the dowry of 1924, which other accounts date to the 1950s, so the story does not say.
The founder (Georges Roumier) and his son are not named for want of searched dates; the grandson who runs the domaine is living and is not named.

wine.name: Clos de Tart
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Nuits since 1939, held whole as a monopole
wine.sites: The walled clos itself, on the Morey-Saint-Denis slope between Clos des Lambrays to the north and Bonnes-Mares to the south, its rows planted across the slope from north to south rather than down it and picked in separate parcels.
wine.making: The parcels of the clos are picked and fermented apart and gathered into pre-blends before they are aged in oak barrels and blended. Wine the domaine judges below the grand cru, from the younger vines among others, is declassified, and the grand cru is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and crushed violet over iron, liquorice and a savoury, stony depth; dark and firmly built, with dense, fine tannin and a long, cool finish.
wine.ageing: Dark and closed young, it opens after about ten years and lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The grand cru, its own appellation, a walled vineyard of Morey-Saint-Denis.
The rank above Premier Cru, printed with the vineyard's name; Clos de Tart has held it since 1939.

records.table: A walled grand cru held whole since Cistercian nuns acquired it in 1141, Clos de Tart is made entirely by the Domaine du Clos de Tart. Its rows run across the slope, and its wine is dark, firm and slow, glad of an hour in a decanter.
records.story: In 1141 the Cistercian nuns of Notre-Dame de Tart acquired a vineyard on the slope of Morey from a hospital house at Brochon; the name Clos de Tart came later. They held it for six and a half centuries, and in all that time it was never divided. The Revolution took it from them, and in 1791 it was sold at auction as national property to the Marey-Monge family, who kept it whole until 1932, when it passed to the Mommessin family, merchants of Mâcon. By a decree of 4 January 1939 it became a grand cru appellation of its own. The Mommessin heirs sold it in 2017 to Artémis Domaines, so that in almost nine centuries the clos has known only a handful of owners. Its vines run across the slope, from north to south, against the usual Burgundian rows, a layout said to hold the soil against erosion, and the domaine picks and ferments its parcels apart before it blends the wine; the younger vines go to a second wine, La Forge de Tart. Candidates learn it as the textbook monopole, with a founding year and a short line of owners; guests meet the dark, firm voice of Morey.

others.name: La Forge de Tart
others.note: The second wine, labelled Morey-Saint-Denis Premier Cru, from the younger vines of the clos.

traps: Clos de Tart is a full monopole; Clos des Lambrays, next door, is a near monopole.
Morey-Saint-Denis holds four grands crus wholly its own, Clos de Tart among them, plus the Morey slice of Bonnes-Mares.
Clos de Tart is not Clos de Vougeot: both are walled Cistercian vineyards, but Vougeot is split among many owners.

report: Rechecked with search on 12 November 2026: the nuns of Notre-Dame de Tart acquiring the vineyard in 1141 from a house at Brochon (sold by the Maison-Dieu in Wikipedia, given by the Hospitallers in Hachette Vins), the name Clos de Tart coming later, the sale of 1791 to the Marey-Monge family, the Mommessins of Mâcon from 1932 and the sale of 2017 to Artémis rest on Wikipedia, Corney and Barrow, Hachette Vins and Decanter, read through search; a few accounts date the last sale to 2018.
The grand cru dates from the decree of 4 January 1939, by the appellation's own specification on the Ministry of Agriculture's site.

The rows north to south across the slope, to hold the soil, rest on Thienpont Wine and The Wine Collective; the neighbours (Lambrays to the north, Bonnes-Mares to the south) on Fine and Rare and Quill and Pad; the parcels, the two pre-blends and the declassifications on Decanter's vertical tasting.
La Forge de Tart is listed as a Morey-Saint-Denis Premier Cru by two merchants; that it comes from the younger vines rests on the library and Decanter's note that young vines are declassified.
The label line Monopole is cut: two merchant listings name the wine Grand Cru Monopole, but no search showed the label's words; the monopole stays in the classification, the traps and the table.

classification and label: Grand Cru since 1939 by the appellation's specification; Monopole, which no search showed printed, is cut from the label and the grand cru line now carries the year.
